## Retro Hardware Troubleshooting: The C1581 Drive

A deep dive into retrocomputing hardware highlights the persistent challenges of sourcing and assembling vintage peripherals. Enthusiast @Olem detailed the iterative process of building a custom C1581 Enhanced floppy drive for Commodore 8-bit systems, designed by COREi64 to run on standard wall power. The project faced three distinct hurdles: first, a messy desk led to the installation of an incorrect, blank 27c128 EPROM; second, the drive suffered from hanging issues caused by faulty 74LS14 logic ICs that passed initial testing but were not authentic parts; and third, initial incompatibility with his C64 was resolved by switching to a C128. Despite these quirks, the drive now functions well. @Olem praised the modernized PCB features, such as perimeter LEDs, and the improved 3D-printed case, underscoring the delicate balance of authenticity versus availability in retro hardware projects.

## AI Economics: Volume Over Margins

The narrative surrounding AI labs is shifting from margin compression to revenue expansion driven by volume. Discussion on Bluesky centers on how falling compute costs are actually driving growth rather than eroding profitability. @Bitey highlighted a chart revealing that while median enterprise AI spending remains low at $11, the top 10% of spenders are generating massive revenue upside, a trend closely watched by Wall Street. @conputer argued that cheaper models are broadening the market for frontier capabilities, allowing labs to maintain profitability through efficiency gains and ancillary products like Astra. Investors are now prioritizing ROI per megawatt of GPU buildout. Projections suggest that by late 2026, the combined annualized revenue of OpenAI and Anthropic could surpass $100B, dwarfing competitors and rivaling major retailers like Target.

## Philosophy in the Age of AI

The relevance of philosophical frameworks in AI development is being re-evaluated. Zach Weinersmith argued that rigorous debates on personhood and ethics are more critical than ever. However, Maria Antoniak countered that engaging with other humanities and social sciences may offer more practical insights than traditional philosophical privilege. Maxim Raginsky refined this debate by distinguishing between analytic and continental philosophy. He noted that continental thought already integrates art and history, whereas the AI community’s dismissal of it often stems from analytic philosophy’s "imitation of rigor." Raginsky argued that this sterile "theory T" approach fails to engage with historical context and practice, suggesting a need for a broader interdisciplinary approach to AI ethics.

## Skepticism on AI Video Continuity

Skepticism remains high regarding AI-generated video’s ability to replace traditional cinematography. @Ed (ed3d.net) challenged the notion that AI video will soon achieve perfect continuity and editability. He argued that AI lacks the "filmic terms" and physical decision-making inherent in traditional filmmaking, such as camera movement on tracks. While acknowledging that AI can generate useful *footage* over time, he questioned its ability to maintain the complex repetition required for coherent narrative editing. The prevailing sentiment is a gap between generating isolated clips and producing "information-carrying" content. Despite technological strides, AI has not yet developed the "robot" agency needed to replicate the nuanced choices of a human cinematographer.

## Gaming: Sonic’s Zone Design

Fan discussion continues to focus on *Sonic Superstars*, specifically the "Big Cucky Press Factory Zone." Highlighted primarily by @Sonic The Hedgeblog on both Bluesky and Tumblr, this zone has garnered notable attention for its unique aesthetic and level design. The repetition of the title across platforms suggests it is a standout feature among players, serving as a focal point for fan discussion regarding the game’s artistic direction and humor.

## Quick Hits

*   **Literary Challenge:** User Elliot on Bluesky suggested it might be time to finally read Laurence Sterne’s *Tristram Shandy*, noting the allure and commitment required to tackle its experimental narrative structure.
*   **Camera Repair:** Reddit user ArjunIndigga69 seeks advice for an old Canon PowerShot A1100IS with a missing rubber DC input panel and a cracked screen, wondering if it can survive two weeks of winter use.
*   **LibreOffice Hiring:** The Document Foundation announced Tamás Zolnai as a new LibreOffice Online developer, marking a significant contribution to the web-based editing project.
*   **Streamer Schedule:** Bsky streamer @VoidBurger announced a return to live streaming *Silent Hill: Townfall* on September 27th, following a one-night skip due to encoding delays. The schedule lists global start times for her Twitch channel.
*   **4chan /gg/ Photography Debates:** The Gear General board is abuzz with discussions on vintage photography. Users debated the merits of Wet Plate photography, with one dismissing modern DSLRs as "DSLR unc." Another thread argued EVFs are a "downgrade" for purists, citing video capability as their only real advantage over Optical Viewfinders (OVFs). A final post clarified that EVF discrepancies usually stem from uncalibrated monitors rather than the cameras themselves.

representative_texts: @Olem (Olem@oldbytes.space) — # commodore  # c1581  # retrocomputing Reason number one was that it needs a ROM chip with the right stuff on it. In my befuddeled state I burned the EPROM, put it aside and made a label for it - and then grabbed another random EPROM lying around on my desk, put on the label on that one and tried using it. No luck with that. Turns out I had tried to use this hilariously fake 27c128 (or is that what it is?) - it's blank and the wrong kind. Took me an hour or so to figure that one out. I need to clean up my messy desk, I guess.

@Olem (Olem@oldbytes.space) — # commodore  # c1581  # retrocomputing The next reason was not on me: The drive powered up all right, but when it was connected to my C128, I would never get a blinking cursor after the READY promt on the computer. It would simply hang. The C128 checks for a bootable disk when it starts, seemed like something failed during that process. After a bit of experimenting I found that the 74LS14s from this batch was the issue. All of them causes the same error. A desoldered 74LS14 from a scrap board fixed the issue right away. The funny thing is that these 74LS14s passes the logic IC test in my MiniPro. So it seems that they are 7414s of some kind, but I guess they're not LS parts...I think Noel from Noels Retro Lab on YouTube had a similiar issue with a logic chp in one of his videos. Seriously, what's the point of faking stuff like this?

@Olem (Olem@oldbytes.space) — # commodore  # c1581  # retrocomputing The third reason was simply a quarrelsome C64. Tried with another machine, and everything was a-ok. Now it works very well with my C128 too. I printed the case for it a while back, but I wasn't too happy with the front. Had another go at that too, and it improved. Printing it at angle is the trick. # 3dprinting

@Olem (Olem@oldbytes.space) — # commodore  # c1581  # retrocomputing Oh, almost forgot to link to the project, COREi64 designed this. The latest PCBs have LEDs all around: https:// github.com/COREi64/1581-Enhanc ed
context_texts: @Olem (Olem@oldbytes.space) — In this week's episode of Why Doesn't The Bloody Thing Work we'll take a look at this thing I just threw together on a whim from parts I had lying around. Well, TBH I had planned to build it sooner or later - it's the 1581 enhanced, a floppy disk drive for Commodore 8-bit machines using the 3.5 inch floppys we all know and love. What makes it special is that it can use normal wall wart for power, it doesn't need that special Commodore PSU with a DIN plug. The drive mech is a modified PC drive, and the case is 3D printed. I'm troubleshooting the freshly soldered mainboard here. Turns there was three reasons for it's nonfunctional state. # commodore  # c1581  # retrocomputing
clusters.summary: Retrocomputing enthusiast @Olem details the troubleshooting process of building a custom C1581 Enhanced floppy drive for Commodore 8-bit machines, designed by COREi64 to operate on standard wall power. He identifies three specific failures: first, using a blank, incorrect 27c128 EPROM due to a messy desk; second, encountering hanging issues caused by faulty 74LS14 logic ICs that passed his MiniPro tester but were not true LS parts; and third, initial incompatibility with his C64, which was resolved by switching to his C128. Olem notes the drive now functions well, praising the improved 3D-printed case design and the modernized PCB features like perimeter LEDs. The cluster highlights the quirks of sourcing authentic vs. fake components in retro hardware projects.

representative_texts: @4530770 - /p/ — /gg/ - gear general — >>4530761 >EVF live view does not show the actual image that will be taken Yes it does. That is the entire point of mirrorless: WYSIWYG (what you see is what you get) If your preview does not match the review, something is wrong with the camera (excepting extreme cases like very short and very long shutter speeds). If what you see in EVF during review does not match your computer monitor you need to calibrate the EVF or monitor, or both. Take a photo of something with full tonal range and colours and have the photo displayed on both the EVF and monitor at the same time, observe and make adjustments until they are matching. Displays shift in colour/brightness over time so a recalibration should be done every couple of years. If you open the the RAW in an editor and it displays very differently from what the camera shows you should get a better RAW editor which actually respects the as-shot settings, or maybe it's just a matter of selecting a proper default profile. RAW software from OEM will generally always match the as-shot camera image.
